entries.knownHazards: Although no mention has been found for this species, some members of this genus contain saponins. Saponins are found in many foods, such as some beans, and although they are fairly toxic to people they are poorly absorbed by the body and most pass straight through without any problem. They are also broken down if the food is thoroughly cooked for a long time. Saponins are much more toxic to some creatures, such as fish, and hunting tribes have traditionally put large quantities of them in streams, lakes etc in order to stupefy or kill the fish[K].
entries.knownHazardsLtV2: Kai kurie šios genties augalai turi saponinų — toksišką žuvims medžiagą; žmonių organizme saponinai prastai absorbuojami ir daugiausia pasišalina nesukeliant žalos. Ilgas virinimas saponinus skaido.
entries.knownHazardsLtEdited: Kai kuriuose šios genties augaluose yra saponinų — žmonių organizme jie prastai pasisavinami ir daugiausia pasišalina be žalos, tačiau žuvims yra toksiški. Ilgas virinimas saponinus skaido.
entries.changesNotes: 'augalai turi saponinų' → 'augaluose yra saponinų' (calque taisymas); 'absorbuojami' → 'pasisavinami' (natūralesnis LT); 'toksišką žuvims medžiagą' pertvarkytas į nuoseklesnę struktūrą; 'nesukeliant žalos' → 'be žalos' (ekonomija).

entries.knownHazards: Although we have found no reports of toxicity for this species, a number of ferns contain carcinogens so some caution is advisable[200]. Many ferns also contain thiaminase, an enzyme that robs the body of its vitamin B complex. In small quantities this enzyme will do no harm to people eating an adequate diet that is rich in vitamin B, though large quantities can cause severe health problems. The enzyme is destroyed by heat or thorough drying, so cooking the plant will remove the thiaminase[172].

entries.knownHazards: The bark, bruised leaves and fruits smell strongly of bitter almonds, suggesting the presence of hydrogen cyanide. They are reputed to be poisonous and are used in witchcraft[418 ]. Hydrogen cyanide is found mainly in the leaves, seed and bark, and is readily detected by its bitter taste. It is usually present in too small a quantity to do any harm but any very bitter seed or fruit should not be eaten. In small quantities, hydrogen cyanide has been shown to stimulate respiration and improve digestion, it is also claimed to be of benefit in the treatment of cancer. In excess, however, it can cause respiratory failure and even death.
